title: Timothy and Epaphroditus (Philippians 2:19–30)
hook: two friends honored: one who cares, one who nearly died serving

segments.voice: Yesterday, a small church told to shine like stars, and your line was shine as lights.

At the end of a film the credits roll: the grip, the caterer, the person who drove the van. Plenty of people are out the door before they finish. A few lines after the great hymn of Christ emptied and lifted up, Paul's letter does something that looks almost ordinary. Travel plans. Two names. A man who has served beside him like a son, and a man from Philippi itself who brought a gift and nearly died delivering it. The letter stops to roll the credits, and Paul reads them out slowly.

First, Timothy. Paul is in chains, and he hopes to send Timothy to Philippi soon. In the King James Bible: "For I have no man likeminded, who will naturally care for your state." Naturally. Not because he's told to. Timothy simply cares. And a family picture: "as a son with the father, he hath served with me in the gospel." Acts says Timothy's mother was a Jewish believer and his father Greek, and that Paul took him along on his travels. Then, Epaphroditus. Everything we know about him is in this letter. The church at Philippi sent him to carry their gift to Paul in prison and to stay and help. Somewhere along the way he fell ill. "For indeed he was sick nigh unto death: but God had mercy on him; and not on him only, but on me also, lest I should have sorrow upon sorrow." Paul doesn't pretend. He would have grieved. And a tender detail: Epaphroditus is homesick and heavy-hearted, not about his illness, but because the people back home heard he was ill, and he hates to think of them worrying. So Paul sends him home: "Receive him therefore in the Lord with all gladness; and hold such in reputation." Modern versions say honor. The courier. The helper. The one who almost didn't make it back. In a letter about Christ lowering himself, Paul shows what that looks like in two ordinary lives, and asks the church to lift them up.
screen: then, large: `RECEIVE HIM WITH ALL GLADNESS.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who helps and is rarely thanked out loud: the person who covers the shift, the neighbor who takes in the packages, the relative who always drives. Remember one specific thing they did, and imagine saying it by name in front of others, short and true, the way Paul did in a letter read aloud to a whole church. If you pray, you can give thanks for them by name.
Epaphroditus. The Philippians' courier who nearly died bringing their gift to Paul in prison, and whom Paul sends home asking the church to hold him in honor.
Your line: hold such in honor. The helpers belong in the story too. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many churches remember helpers by name in their prayers and announcements, and some traditions honor Timothy and other companions of Paul with feast days in the church calendar.

fork.setup: you're Paul, in chains. your friend Epaphroditus has recovered from a near-fatal illness and is homesick. what do you do?
options: keep him with you, since you need help.
send him home, and tell the church to honor him.
fork.reveal: Paul sends him home and asks the church to "receive him therefore in the Lord with all gladness; and hold such in reputation."

original.note: Greek: held in honor, precious. it comes from timē, honor, the same root as the name Timothy.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of travel plans in the middle of a letter.
what it means: Paul stops to honor two helpers, one who cares and one who nearly died serving.
what a scholar hears: the passage follows straight after the hymn of Christ emptying himself, and some read Timothy and Epaphroditus as living examples of that same lowering.
recall: the world: loved by God, often hostile

chat.says: Why would Paul spend part of a letter on travel plans and a sick messenger?
options: To honor two helpers by name, and ask the church to receive them gladly.
To explain why Epaphroditus quit early and was sent home in disgrace.
To warn the church that Timothy would come and check on their behavior.
chat.meaning: Paul praises Timothy and Epaphroditus and asks the church to "hold such in reputation": honor the helpers.

Epaphroditus.meaning: the Philippians' courier who brought their gift to Paul

Timothy.meaning: Paul's co-worker, who served with him like a son

Philippi.meaning: the Roman colony whose church Paul writes to

Acts.meaning: the Bible book that tells of the first churches

notes: The carry 'hold such in honor' follows modern renderings; the KJV of Philippians 2:29 reads 'hold such in reputation'. The script gives both.
Epaphroditus's name is commonly linked to Aphrodite; the inference that his family may have worshiped the Greek gods is softened to 'may well have'. Confirm.
Acts 16:1 says Timothy's mother was a Jewish believer and his father a Greek. Confirm wording.
Original: ἔντιμος appears in Philippians 2:29 (ἐντίμους ἔχετε); its root link to τιμή and the name Τιμόθεος is standard but should be checked.
Paul's imprisonment location (Rome, Ephesus or Caesarea) is debated and deliberately left unnamed.
